\section{Systems of Linear Equations}

\begin{note}
\textbf{Learning outcomes.} By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
\begin{itemize}
  \item solve a two variable linear system by elimination;
  \item describe the three elementary row operations;
  \item determine whether a linear system is consistent, inconsistent or has infinitely many solutions;
  \item recognise a homogeneous system and state the nature of its solutions;
  \item write a linear system in augmented matrix form and interpret its rows.
\end{itemize}
\end{note}

\subsection{Solving by elimination}

A system of two linear equations in two unknowns can be written as
\[
a_{1}x+b_{1}y=c_{1},\qquad a_{2}x+b_{2}y=c_{2}.
\]
The elimination method removes one variable by adding a suitable multiple of one equation to the other. Choose a multiplier that makes the coefficients of the chosen variable equal in magnitude but opposite in sign. After the variable cancels, solve the remaining single variable equation and back substitute to obtain the other variable.

\begin{example}
Solve
\[
2x+3y=8,\qquad 5x-3y=7.
\]
Add the two equations because the $y$ terms cancel:
\[
(2x+3y)+(5x-3y)=8+7\Longrightarrow 7x=15\Longrightarrow x=\tfrac{15}{7}.
\]
Substitute $x$ into the first equation:
\[
2\!\left(\tfrac{15}{7}\right)+3y=8\Longrightarrow \tfrac{30}{7}+3y=8\Longrightarrow 3y=8-\tfrac{30}{7}
=\tfrac{26}{7}\Longrightarrow y=\tfrac{26}{21}.
\]
Thus the solution is $\bigl(\tfrac{15}{7},\tfrac{26}{21}\bigr)$.
\end{example}

If the coefficients of the chosen variable are not already opposites, multiply one or both equations by suitable constants before adding. The essential idea is to create a zero coefficient for one variable, solve for the remaining variable, then back substitute.

\subsection{Row operations}

When a system has more than two equations or more than two variables, writing the equations in a matrix and using row operations is more systematic. The three elementary row operations are:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \term{Row swap}: interchange two rows.
  \item \term{Scalar multiplication}: multiply a row by a non zero constant.
  \item \term{Row replacement}: replace a row by the sum of itself and a multiple of another row.
\end{itemize}

These operations do not change the solution set of the system. They are used to transform the augmented matrix into \term{row echelon form} or \term{reduced row echelon form}, from which the solutions are read directly.

\begin{example}
Consider the system
\[
\begin{aligned}
x+2y- z &= 4,\\
2x+ y+3z &= 1,\\
- x+ y+2z &= -3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Write the augmented matrix:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & -1 & \vline & 4\\
2 & 1 &  3 & \vline & 1\\
-1& 1 &  2 & \vline & -3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

\textbf{Step 1:} Use row replacement to eliminate the $x$ term in rows 2 and 3.
\[
R_{2}\leftarrow R_{2}-2R_{1},\quad
R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}+R_{1}.
\]
Result:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & -1 & \vline & 4\\
0 & -3 & 5 & \vline & -7\\
0 & 3 & 1 & \vline & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

\textbf{Step 2:} Swap rows 2 and 3 to obtain a positive pivot.
\[
R_{2}\leftrightarrow R_{3}.
\]
Result:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & -1 & \vline & 4\\
0 & 3 & 1 & \vline & 1\\
0 & -3 & 5 & \vline & -7
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

\textbf{Step 3:} Eliminate the $y$ term in row 3.
\[
R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}+R_{2}.
\]
Result:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & -1 & \vline & 4\\
0 & 3 & 1 & \vline & 1\\
0 & 0 & 6 & \vline & -6
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

\textbf{Step 4:} Scale row 3.
\[
R_{3}\leftarrow \tfrac{1}{6}R_{3}.
\]
Result:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & -1 & \vline & 4\\
0 & 3 & 1 & \vline & 1\\
0 & 0 & 1 & \vline & -1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Back substitution gives $z=-1$, then $3y+(-1)=1\Rightarrow y=\tfrac{2}{3}$, and finally $x+2(\tfrac{2}{3})-(-1)=4\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{7}{3}$. The unique solution is $\bigl(\tfrac{7}{3},\tfrac{2}{3},-1\bigr)$.
\end{example}

\subsection{Consistency of a system}

A linear system is \term{consistent} if it has at least one solution; otherwise it is \term{inconsistent}. After row reduction, consistency can be read from the augmented matrix:

\begin{itemize}
  \item A row of the form $[0\;0\;\dots\;0\mid b]$ with $b\neq0$ indicates inconsistency because it represents the impossible equation $0=b$.
  \item If no such contradictory row appears, the system is consistent.
  \item When the number of pivots (leading non zero entries) equals the number of variables, the consistent system has a unique solution.
  \item When there are fewer pivots than variables, the system has infinitely many solutions, described by free variables.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Homogeneous systems}

A system is called \term{homogeneous} when every equation has zero on the right hand side. In matrix form the augmented column is a column of zeros. Homogeneous systems are always consistent because the trivial solution, where all variables are zero, satisfies every equation. The interest lies in whether there are non trivial solutions.

If the coefficient matrix has fewer pivots than variables, at least one variable is free and the system possesses infinitely many solutions, including non trivial ones. If the number of pivots equals the number of variables, the only solution is the trivial one.

\begin{example}
Solve the homogeneous system
\[
\begin{aligned}
x+ y+ z &= 0,\\
2x+3y+ z &= 0,\\
- x+ y+2z &= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Write the augmented matrix (the last column is all zeros):
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 1 & \vline & 0\\
2 & 3 & 1 & \vline & 0\\
-1& 1 & 2 & \vline & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

\textbf{Step 1:} Replace $R_{2}\leftarrow R_{2}-2R_{1}$ and $R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}+R_{1}$.
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 1 & \vline & 0\\
0 & 1 & -1 & \vline & 0\\
0 & 2 & 3 & \vline & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

\textbf{Step 2:} Replace $R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}-2R_{2}$.
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 1 & \vline & 0\\
0 & 1 & -1 & \vline & 0\\
0 & 0 & 5 & \vline & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

\textbf{Step 3:} Scale $R_{3}\leftarrow \tfrac{1}{5}R_{3}$.
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 1 & \vline & 0\\
0 & 1 & -1 & \vline & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1 & \vline & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Back substitution yields $z=0$, then $y-0=0\Rightarrow y=0$, and finally $x+0+0=0\Rightarrow x=0$. The only solution is the trivial one $(0,0,0)$. Because the coefficient matrix has a pivot in every column, no free variables appear.
\end{example}

\subsection{Augmented matrix representation}

Any linear system can be expressed as an augmented matrix. Each row corresponds to one equation; the entries before the vertical bar are the coefficients of the variables, and the entry after the bar is the constant term. This compact form makes it easy to apply row operations and to recognise special patterns.

For example, the system
\[
\begin{aligned}
3x-2y+z &= 5,\\
- x+4y-2z &= -3,
\end{aligned}
\]
is represented by
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
3 & -2 & 1 & \vline & 5\\
-1& 4 & -2 & \vline & -3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Reading the matrix, the first row tells us that $3$ multiplies $x$, $-2$ multiplies $y$, $1$ multiplies $z$, and the constant on the right is $5$. The second row is interpreted similarly. Once the matrix is written, the three elementary row operations can be performed directly on the rows, without rewriting the equations each time. After reduction, the resulting matrix can be translated back into equations to read the solution.

\begin{keytest}
\textbf{Key test.} For each of the following systems, perform row reduction and state whether the system is consistent, and if so whether the solution is unique or infinite:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $\begin{cases}x+ y=2\\ 2x+2y=4\end{cases}$
  \item $\begin{cases}x- y=1\\ 3x-3y=5\end{cases}$
  \item $\begin{cases}x+2y+z=3\\ 2x+4y+2z=6\\ -x-2y-z=-3\end{cases}$
\end{enumerate}
\end{keytest}

\subsection{Exercises}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Solve the system $3x-4y=5$, $6x-8y=10$ by elimination. Explain the result.
  \item Use row operations to solve
  \[
  \begin{cases}
  2x+ y- z=1\\
  -x+3y+2z=4\\
  4x-2y+5z=7.
  \end{cases}
  \]
  Show each elementary operation.
  \item Determine the consistency of the system
  \[
  \begin{cases}
  x+2y+3z=6\\
  2x+4y+6z=12\\
  -x-2y-3z=-5.
  \end{cases}
  \]
  Justify your answer using row reduction.
  \item Solve the homogeneous system
  \[
  \begin{cases}
  x-2y+z=0\\
  3x-6y+3z=0.
  \end{cases}
  \]
  Describe the set of solutions.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Key terms}

\begin{tabular}{@{}p{3.6cm}p{10.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Term} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\midrule
Elimination & Adding a multiple of one equation to another to cancel a variable. \\
Row operation & One of the three elementary manipulations of rows that preserve solutions. \\
Row echelon form & A matrix form with leading ones stepping to the right in each lower row. \\
Consistent system & A system that has at least one solution. \\
Inconsistent system & A system that has no solution, usually revealed by a contradictory row. \\
Homogeneous system & A linear system whose right hand side is all zeros; always has the trivial solution. \\
Augmented matrix & A rectangular array that records the coefficients of the variables and the constants of a linear system. \\
Unique solution & Exactly one ordered tuple satisfies all equations. \\
Infinite solutions & More than one solution; free variables describe a family of solutions. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\section{Matrices}

\begin{note}
\textbf{Learning outcomes.} By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
\begin{itemize}
  \item perform the basic matrix operations of addition, subtraction and multiplication;
  \item compute the inverse of a square matrix when it exists;
  \item calculate the determinant of a square matrix and interpret its meaning;
  \item recognise situations where a matrix is singular and cannot be inverted;
  \item apply the transpose operation and identify symmetric matrices.
\end{itemize}
\end{note}

\subsection{Matrix notation and basic operations}

A \term{matrix} is a rectangular array of numbers written inside brackets. The entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is denoted $a_{ij}$. A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns is called an $m\times n$ matrix.

Two matrices $A$ and $B$ can be added only if they have the same dimensions. The sum $C=A+B$ is obtained by adding corresponding entries:
\[
c_{ij}=a_{ij}+b_{ij}.
\]
Subtraction works in the same way.

Multiplication of matrices is defined differently. If $A$ is $m\times p$ and $B$ is $p\times n$, the product $C=AB$ is an $m\times n$ matrix whose entries are
\[
c_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{p}a_{ik}b_{kj}.
\]
The number of columns of the first factor must equal the number of rows of the second factor. Matrix multiplication is not commutative; in general $AB\neq BA$.

A matrix multiplied by a scalar $k$ is formed by multiplying each entry by $k$: $(kA)_{ij}=k\,a_{ij}$.

\begin{example}
Let 
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}5&6\\7&8\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Then $A+B=\begin{bmatrix}6&8\\10&12\end{bmatrix}$.
For the product,
\[
AB=\begin{bmatrix}
1\cdot5+2\cdot7 & 1\cdot6+2\cdot8\\
3\cdot5+4\cdot7 & 3\cdot6+4\cdot8
\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}19&22\\43&50\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Note that $BA=\begin{bmatrix}23&34\\31&46\end{bmatrix}$, which is different from $AB$.
\end{example}

\subsection{The identity matrix and matrix powers}

The \term{identity matrix} $I_n$ is the $n\times n$ matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere. For any $n\times n$ matrix $A$, we have $AI_n=I_nA=A$.

If $A$ is square, we can define powers $A^k$ by repeated multiplication: $A^2=AA$, $A^3=AAA$, and so on. By convention $A^0=I_n$.

\subsection{Inverses of square matrices}

A square matrix $A$ is \term{invertible} (or \term{nonsingular}) if there exists a matrix $A^{-1}$ such that
\[
AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I_n.
\]
If such a matrix exists, it is unique. A matrix that is not invertible is called \term{singular}.

For a $2\times2$ matrix 
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix},
\]
the inverse exists precisely when $ad-bc\neq0$. In that case
\[
A^{-1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}.
\]

For larger matrices, the inverse can be found by row reducing the augmented matrix $[A\mid I_n]$ to $[I_n\mid A^{-1}]$, or by using the adjugate formula
\[
A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det A}\,\operatorname{adj}(A),
\]
provided $\det A\neq0$.

\begin{example}
Consider 
\[
C=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The determinant is $2\cdot3-1\cdot5=6-5=1\neq0$, so $C$ is invertible. Using the $2\times2$ formula,
\[
C^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-5&2\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-5&2\end{bmatrix}.
\]
A quick check shows $CC^{-1}=I_2$.
\end{example}

\subsection{Determinants}

The \term{determinant} is a scalar value assigned to a square matrix. It provides information about volume scaling, invertibility, and eigenvalues.

For a $1\times1$ matrix $[a]$, $\det[a]=a$. For a $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}$, $\det =ad-bc$.

For a $3\times3$ matrix 
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
a&b&c\\
d&e&f\\
g&h&i
\end{bmatrix},
\]
the determinant can be computed by cofactor expansion along the first row:
\[
\det =a\begin{vmatrix}e&f\\h&i\end{vmatrix}
-b\begin{vmatrix}d&f\\g&i\end{vmatrix}
+c\begin{vmatrix}d&e\\g&h\end{vmatrix}.
\]

Key properties:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $\det(AB)=\det A\;\det B$.
  \item Swapping two rows changes the sign of the determinant.
  \item Multiplying a row by a scalar $k$ multiplies the determinant by $k$.
  \item A matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is zero.
\end{itemize}

\begin{example}
Find the determinant of 
\[
D=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\0&4&5\\1&0&6\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Expanding along the second row (which contains a zero) gives
\[
\det D = -4\begin{vmatrix}1&3\\1&6\end{vmatrix}
= -4(1\cdot6-3\cdot1) = -4(6-3) = -12.
\]
Since $\det D\neq0$, $D$ is invertible.
\end{example}

\subsection{Transpose and symmetric matrices}

The \term{transpose} of a matrix $A$, denoted $A^{\mathsf T}$, is obtained by reflecting $A$ across its main diagonal. Formally, the entry in row $i$, column $j$ of $A^{\mathsf T}$ equals the entry in row $j$, column $i$ of $A$.

A matrix is \term{symmetric} if it equals its own transpose, that is $A=A^{\mathsf T}$. Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and are central in many applications.

\begin{example}
Let 
\[
E=\begin{bmatrix}1&4&7\\2&5&8\\3&6&9\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Its transpose is 
\[
E^{\mathsf T}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&8&9\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Since $E\neq E^{\mathsf T}$, $E$ is not symmetric. By contrast, the matrix 
\[
F=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&3&4\\0&4&5\end{bmatrix}
\]
satisfies $F^{\mathsf T}=F$, so $F$ is symmetric.
\end{example}

\subsection{Singular matrices and the role of the determinant}

If $\det A=0$, the matrix $A$ does not have an inverse. Geometrically, the linear transformation represented by $A$ collapses the $n$ dimensional space into a lower dimensional subspace, so volumes are mapped to zero.

A common test for singularity is to row reduce $A$ to echelon form. If a row of zeros appears, the matrix is singular.

\begin{keytest}
\textbf{Key test.} Given a square matrix $M$, compute $\det M$. If the result is non zero, write down the formula for $M^{-1}$ (for $2\times2$) or set up the augmented matrix $[M\mid I]$ and row reduce. If the determinant is zero, state that $M$ is singular and has no inverse.
\end{keytest}

\subsection{Exercises}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Add and multiply the matrices $G=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $H=\begin{bmatrix}3&4\\5&6\end{bmatrix}$. Verify that $GH\neq HG$.
  \item Compute the inverse of $J=\begin{bmatrix}4&7\\2&6\end{bmatrix}$ using the $2\times2$ formula.
  \item Find the determinant of $K=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&0\\3&4&5\\1&0&-2\end{bmatrix}$ and decide whether $K$ is invertible.
  \item Determine whether the matrix $L=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\\3&6&9\end{bmatrix}$ is singular by row reduction.
  \item For the matrix $M=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&3&4\\0&4&5\end{bmatrix}$, compute $M^{\mathsf T}$ and state whether $M$ is symmetric.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Key terms}

\begin{tabular}{@{}p{3.6cm}p{10.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Term} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\midrule
Matrix & Rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. \\
Identity matrix & Square matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere. \\
Inverse matrix & Matrix $A^{-1}$ such that $AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I$, exists only for nonsingular square matrices. \\
Singular matrix & Square matrix with determinant zero; it has no inverse. \\
Determinant & Scalar value that summarises scaling and invertibility properties of a square matrix. \\
Transpose & Matrix obtained by swapping rows and columns; denoted $A^{\mathsf T}$. \\
Symmetric matrix & Square matrix that equals its own transpose. \\
Row reduction & Sequence of elementary row operations used to transform a matrix to echelon form. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\lessonlabel{3}
\section{Vector Spaces}

\begin{note}
\textbf{Learning outcomes.} By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
\begin{itemize}
  \item describe what a vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$ looks like and how to add and scale vectors;
  \item define a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and verify the subspace criteria;
  \item explain the concept of linear independence and test a set of vectors for independence;
  \item state what a basis of a subspace is and how it relates to dimension;
  \item apply these ideas to simple problems in geometry and algebra.
\end{itemize}
\end{note}

\subsection{Vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$}

A \term{vector} in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an ordered list of $n$ real numbers. We write it as a column
\[
\mathbf{v}= \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ \vdots \\ v_n \end{bmatrix},
\]
or as a row $(v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n)$. The number $n$ is called the \term{dimension} of the space. For example, a point in the plane is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^2$, while a point in three dimensional space is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Two basic operations are defined for all vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Addition.} If $\mathbf{u}=(u_1,\dots ,u_n)$ and $\mathbf{v}=(v_1,\dots ,v_n)$, then
  \[
  \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}= (u_1+v_1,\dots ,u_n+v_n).
  \]
  The result is again a vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
  \item \textbf{Scalar multiplication.} If $c$ is a real number and $\mathbf{v}=(v_1,\dots ,v_n)$, then
  \[
  c\mathbf{v}= (cv_1,\dots ,cv_n).
  \]
  This also yields a vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
\end{itemize}

These operations satisfy the familiar algebraic rules of commutativity, associativity, distributivity and the existence of a zero vector $\mathbf{0}=(0,\dots ,0)$ that leaves any vector unchanged when added.

\begin{example}
Let $\mathbf{a}= (2,-1,3)$ and $\mathbf{b}= (0,4,-2)$ be vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Their sum is
\[
\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}= (2+0,\,-1+4,\,3-2)= (2,3,1).
\]
If we multiply $\mathbf{a}$ by the scalar $-2$, we obtain
\[
-2\mathbf{a}= (-4,2,-6).
\]
Both results are still vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
\end{example}

\subsection{Subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^n$}

A \term{subspace} of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a subset $W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ that is itself a vector space under the same addition and scalar multiplication. To check whether a set $W$ is a subspace we use three simple criteria:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item The zero vector $\mathbf{0}$ belongs to $W$.
  \item $W$ is closed under addition: if $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in W$, then $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\in W$.
  \item $W$ is closed under scalar multiplication: if $\mathbf{u}\in W$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$, then $c\mathbf{u}\in W$.
\end{enumerate}

If any of these fails, $W$ is not a subspace.

Common examples include the whole space $\mathbb{R}^n$, the set of vectors whose last coordinate is zero (a plane through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$), and the solution set of a homogeneous linear system $A\mathbf{x}= \mathbf{0}$.

\begin{example}
Consider the set $W=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3\mid x+2y-3z=0\}$.

\textbf{Zero vector.} Substituting $x=y=z=0$ gives $0+0-0=0$, so $\mathbf{0}\in W$.

\textbf{Addition.} Let $\mathbf{u}=(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $\mathbf{v}=(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ satisfy the equation. Then
\[
(x_1+x_2)+2(y_1+y_2)-3(z_1+z_2)= (x_1+2y_1-3z_1)+(x_2+2y_2-3z_2)=0+0=0,
\]
so $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\in W$.

\textbf{Scalar multiplication.} For any scalar $c$,
\[
c x_1+2c y_1-3c z_1 = c(x_1+2y_1-3z_1)=c\cdot 0=0,
\]
hence $c\mathbf{u}\in W$.

All three conditions hold, so $W$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$. Geometrically it is a plane through the origin.
\end{example}

\subsection{Linear Independence}

A finite set of vectors $\{\mathbf{v}_1,\dots ,\mathbf{v}_k\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is \term{linearly independent} if the only way to combine them to obtain the zero vector is the trivial combination
\[
c_1\mathbf{v}_1+\cdots +c_k\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{0}
\quad\text{implies}\quad
c_1=c_2=\dots =c_k=0.
\]
If there exists a non trivial choice of scalars (not all zero) that yields $\mathbf{0}$, the set is \term{linearly dependent}.

Intuitively, independent vectors point in genuinely different directions; none can be written as a combination of the others.

A practical test uses a matrix. Place the vectors as columns of a matrix $A$. The set is independent exactly when the only solution to $A\mathbf{c}= \mathbf{0}$ is $\mathbf{c}= \mathbf{0}$. In other words, the matrix must have a pivot in every column.

\begin{example}
Take $\mathbf{u}= (1,2,0)$, $\mathbf{v}= (3,6,0)$, and $\mathbf{w}= (0,0,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Form the matrix
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 3 & 0\\
2 & 6 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Row reducing, subtract three times column 1 from column 2 to obtain a zero column:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
2 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

The second column becomes the zero vector, showing that $\mathbf{v}=3\mathbf{u}$. Hence $\{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\}$ is linearly dependent. Removing $\mathbf{v}$ leaves $\{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w}\}$, which is independent because the reduced matrix now has pivots in both columns.
\end{example}

\subsection{Basis and Dimension}

A \term{basis} of a subspace $W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is a set of vectors in $W$ that is linearly independent and spans $W$. ``Spanning'' means that every vector in $W$ can be expressed as a linear combination of the basis vectors. The number of vectors in any basis of $W$ is called the \term{dimension} of $W$.

To verify that a set $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of $W$ we must check two things:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Independence.} Use the matrix test described above.
  \item \textbf{Spanning.} Show that an arbitrary vector $\mathbf{w}\in W$ can be written as a combination of the vectors in $\mathcal{B}$.
\end{itemize}

If $W$ is the whole space $\mathbb{R}^n$, a standard basis is $\{ \mathbf{e}_1,\dots ,\mathbf{e}_n\}$ where $\mathbf{e}_i$ has a $1$ in the $i$th position and $0$ elsewhere. Any other basis will have exactly $n$ vectors, confirming that the dimension of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $n$.

\begin{keytest}
\textbf{Key test.} Given vectors $\mathbf{a}= (1,0,-2)$, $\mathbf{b}= (0,1,3)$ and $\mathbf{c}= (2,1,-1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, decide whether they span a subspace, and whether they are linearly independent. Show your work using the subspace criteria and a matrix test.
\end{keytest}

\subsection{Exercises}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Write three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^4$ and compute their sum and the result of multiplying one of them by $-3$.
  \item Let $W=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3\mid x-y+z=0\}$. Verify that $W$ satisfies the three subspace criteria.
  \item Determine whether the set $\{(1,2,1),\;(2,4,2),\;(0,1,0)\}$ is linearly independent. Explain each step.
  \item Find a basis for the subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$ consisting of all vectors whose third component is zero.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Key terms}

\begin{tabular}{@{}p{3.6cm}p{10.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Term} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\midrule
Vector & An ordered $n$ tuple of real numbers, written as a column or row, representing a point or direction in $\mathbb{R}^n$. \\
$\mathbb{R}^n$ & The set of all $n$ dimensional real vectors; a standard example of a vector space. \\
Subspace & A subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ that contains the zero vector and is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication. \\
Linear independence & A property of a set of vectors where the only linear combination that gives the zero vector uses all zero coefficients. \\
Linear dependence & The opposite of independence; some non trivial combination of the vectors yields the zero vector. \\
Basis & A set of linearly independent vectors that spans a subspace; every vector in the subspace can be expressed uniquely as a combination of basis vectors. \\
Dimension & The number of vectors in any basis of a subspace; it measures the size of the space. \\
Span & The collection of all linear combinations of a given set of vectors; the smallest subspace containing those vectors. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\lessonlabel{5}
\section{Linear Transformations}

\begin{note}
\textbf{Learning outcomes.} By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
\begin{itemize}
  \item write a linear transformation as a matrix and interpret the entries;
  \item define the kernel and the range of a linear transformation and compute them from a matrix;
  \item state and use the rank--nullity relation for a linear transformation;
  \item describe how a linear transformation acts on the standard basis vectors;
  \item understand how the composition of two linear transformations is represented by matrix multiplication.
\end{itemize}
\end{note}

\subsection{Matrix representation}

A \term{linear transformation} is a rule that takes a vector in a domain space and returns a vector in a codomain space while preserving addition and scalar multiplication.  When the domain is the space of n tuples and the codomain is the space of m tuples, we can describe the transformation completely by an m by n array of numbers.  This array is called the \term{matrix representation} of the transformation.

To build the matrix, start with the standard basis vectors of the domain: \(e_{1}=(1,0,\dots ,0)\), \(e_{2}=(0,1,0,\dots ,0)\), and so on up to \(e_{n}\).  Apply the transformation to each basis vector.  The resulting vectors are m dimensional column vectors.  Place these columns side by side in the same order; the resulting array is the matrix \(A\).  For every input vector \(x\), the output is obtained by the matrix vector product \(A\,x\).

The entry \(a_{ij}\) tells how much of the i th output coordinate comes from the j th input coordinate.  If a column is the zero vector, the corresponding input direction is collapsed to the origin.  If two columns are multiples of each other, the two input directions produce parallel output directions, indicating linear dependence among the columns.

\begin{example}
Let \(T\colon\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}\) be defined by \(T(x,y,z)=(x+2y,\,3y-z)\).  Compute the matrix of \(T\) with respect to the standard bases.

We evaluate \(T\) on the three basis vectors:
\[
T(1,0,0)=(1,0),\qquad
T(0,1,0)=(2,3),\qquad
T(0,0,1)=(0,-1).
\]
These become the columns of \(A\):
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0\\
0 & 3 & -1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Now \(T(x,y,z)=A\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{bmatrix}\) for any \((x,y,z)\).
\end{example}

\subsection{Action on the standard basis}

Because each column of the representing matrix is the image of a standard basis vector, the whole transformation is determined by these images.  Looking at the columns gives immediate geometric insight.  A zero column means the corresponding input axis is sent to the origin.  Two identical columns mean that two different input directions are merged into the same output direction.  A column that is a scalar multiple of another indicates that the transformation stretches or shrinks one direction in the same way as another.

These observations help to recognise common geometric operations.  For instance, a matrix whose first column is \((1,0)^{T}\) and second column is \((0,0)^{T}\) projects every vector onto the x axis.  A matrix with columns \((0,1)^{T}\) and \((1,0)^{T}\) swaps the x and y coordinates, producing a reflection across the line \(y=x\).

\subsection{Kernel and range}

The \term{kernel} (or null space) of a linear transformation \(T\) is the set of all input vectors that are sent to the zero vector in the codomain.  Symbolically,
\[
\ker T=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\mid T(x)=0\}.
\]
When \(T\) is represented by a matrix \(A\), the kernel consists of all solutions of the homogeneous linear system \(A\,x=0\).  Solving this system yields a description of the kernel as a span of certain vectors.

The \term{range} (or image) of \(T\) is the collection of all vectors that actually appear as outputs:
\[
\operatorname{range} T=\{T(x)\mid x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\}.
\]
In matrix terms, the range is the column space of \(A\), that is, the span of the columns of \(A\).  The dimension of the range is called the rank of \(T\).

\begin{example}
Consider the matrix
\[
B=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3\\
2 & 4 & 6
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Find \(\ker T\) and \(\operatorname{range} T\) for the transformation \(T(x)=B\,x\).

First solve \(B\,x=0\):
\[
\begin{cases}
x_{1}+2x_{2}+3x_{3}=0\\
2x_{1}+4x_{2}+6x_{3}=0
\end{cases}
\]
The second equation is twice the first, so there is one independent equation.  Let \(x_{2}=s\) and \(x_{3}=t\).  Then \(x_{1}=-2s-3t\).  Hence
\[
\ker T=\{\,(-2s-3t,\;s,\;t)\mid s,t\in\mathbb{R}\,\}
      =\operatorname{span}\{(-2,1,0),\,(-3,0,1)\}.
\]

The columns of \(B\) are \((1,2)^{T}\), \((2,4)^{T}\), \((3,6)^{T}\), all multiples of \((1,2)^{T}\).  Therefore the column space is one dimensional:
\[
\operatorname{range} T=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2)^{T}\}.
\]
\end{example}

\subsection{Rank}

The \term{rank} of a matrix \(A\) is the dimension of its column space, i.e., the number of linearly independent columns.  For a linear transformation \(T\), the rank of \(T\) is defined as the rank of any matrix that represents \(T\).

Rank measures how many independent directions in the domain are sent to independent directions in the codomain.  It also equals the dimension of the range:
\[
\dim(\operatorname{range} T)=\operatorname{rank} T.
\]

The \term{nullity} of \(T\) is the dimension of its kernel.  The fundamental relationship between rank and nullity is the \term{rank--nullity theorem}:
\[
\operatorname{rank} T+\operatorname{nullity} T=n,
\]
where \(n\) is the dimension of the domain.

\begin{example}
Let
\[
C=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 2\\
0 & 1 & -1\\
3 & 2 & 5
\end{bmatrix}
\]
represent \(T\colon\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{3}\).  Row reduce \(C\):
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 2\\
0 & 1 & -1\\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
There are two non zero rows, so \(\operatorname{rank} T=2\).  Consequently \(\operatorname{nullity} T=3-2=1\).

From the reduced system \(x_{1}+2x_{3}=0\), \(x_{2}-x_{3}=0\) we set \(x_{3}=t\) and obtain \(x_{1}=-2t\), \(x_{2}=t\).  Thus
\[
\ker T=\operatorname{span}\{(-2,1,1)\}.
\]

The range is spanned by the first two columns of \(C\), namely \((1,0,3)^{T}\) and \((0,1,2)^{T}\), a two dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^{3}\).
\end{example}

\subsection{Nullity}

The \term{nullity} of a linear transformation is the number of free parameters in the solution of \(A\,x=0\).  It equals the dimension of the kernel and can be read directly from a reduced row echelon form: nullity is the number of columns that do not contain a leading pivot.  Because rank plus nullity equals the number of columns, knowing one of the two quantities immediately gives the other.

For example, if a matrix has three columns and its reduced form shows two pivot columns, the rank is two and the nullity is one.  This tells us that the transformation collapses the three dimensional domain onto a two dimensional range, leaving a one dimensional subspace of inputs that are sent to the zero vector.

\subsection{Composition of linear transformations}

If \(S\colon\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}\) and \(T\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{p}\) are linear transformations with matrix representations \(A\) (size \(m\times p\)) and \(B\) (size \(p\times n\)) respectively, then the composition \(S\circ T\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}\) is also linear.  Its matrix representation is the product \(A\,B\).  This follows because for any vector \(x\),
\[
(S\circ T)(x)=S(T(x))=A\,(B\,x)=(A\,B)\,x.
\]

The product \(A\,B\) is defined exactly when the number of columns of \(A\) equals the number of rows of \(B\), which matches the requirement that the codomain of \(T\) equals the domain of \(S\).  The rank of the composition cannot exceed the smaller of the ranks of the two factors, reflecting the fact that a composition cannot create more independent output directions than either transformation alone.

\begin{example}
Let \(T\colon\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{3}\) be represented by
\[
B=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0\\
0 & 1\\
1 & 1
\end{bmatrix},
\]
and let \(S\colon\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}\) be represented by
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
2 & -1 & 0\\
0 & 3 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Compute the matrix of \(S\circ T\).

Multiply \(A\) and \(B\):
\[
A\,B=
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & -1 & 0\\
0 & 3 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0\\
0 & 1\\
1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2\cdot1+(-1)\cdot0+0\cdot1 & 2\cdot0+(-1)\cdot1+0\cdot1\\
0\cdot1+3\cdot0+1\cdot1 & 0\cdot0+3\cdot1+1\cdot1
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & -1\\
1 & 4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Thus \((S\circ T)(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1\\1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}\).
\end{example}

\begin{keytest}
\textbf{Key test.} Given a matrix \(A\), determine the linear transformation it defines, compute \(\ker T\) and \(\operatorname{range} T\), verify the rank--nullity relation, and, if a second matrix \(B\) is provided, find the matrix of the composition \(T\circ S\).
\end{keytest}

\subsection{Exercises}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Find the matrix of the transformation \(T(x,y)=(3x-y,\,2y)\) and state its kernel and range.
  \item For the matrix \(D=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{bmatrix}\), compute rank, nullity and a basis for the kernel.
  \item Verify the rank--nullity theorem for the transformation represented by \(E=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\).
  \item Let \(S\) be represented by \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&2\\0&1&-1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(T\) by \(B=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&3\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\).  Compute the matrix of \(S\circ T\).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Key terms}

\begin{tabular}{@{}p{3.6cm}p{10.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Term} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\midrule
Linear transformation & A rule between vector spaces that preserves addition and scalar multiplication. \\
Matrix representation & The array whose columns are the images of the domain basis vectors. \\
Kernel (null space) & Set of all input vectors that map to the zero vector; solution set of \(A\,x=0\). \\
Range (image) & Set of all output vectors; the column space of the representing matrix. \\
Rank & Dimension of the column space; number of linearly independent columns. \\
Nullity & Dimension of the kernel; number of free variables in \(A\,x=0\). \\
Rank--nullity theorem & Relation \(\operatorname{rank}T+\operatorname{nullity}T=n\) for a transformation \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}\). \\
Composition & The operation \(S\circ T\) where the matrix of the composition is the product of the matrices of \(S\) and \(T\). \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\lessonlabel{6}
\section{Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors}

\begin{note}
\textbf{Learning outcomes.} By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
\begin{itemize}
  \item define the characteristic polynomial of a square matrix;
  \item compute eigenvalues by solving the characteristic equation;
  \item find eigenvectors corresponding to each eigenvalue;
  \item state the conditions under which a matrix is diagonalizable;
  \item construct a diagonal matrix that is similar to a given matrix;
  \item explain the role of similarity transformations in diagonalisation.
\end{itemize}
\end{note}

\subsection{Characteristic polynomial}

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix. The \term{characteristic polynomial} of $A$ is the polynomial
\[
p_{A}(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda I),
\]
where $I$ is the $n\times n$ identity matrix and $\lambda$ is an indeterminate. The matrix $A-\lambda I$ is obtained by subtracting $\lambda$ from each diagonal entry of $A$ while leaving the off diagonal entries unchanged. Expanding the determinant yields a polynomial of degree $n$ in $\lambda$. The roots of $p_{A}(\lambda)$ are called the \term{eigenvalues} of $A$.

For a $2\times2$ matrix
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix},
\]
the characteristic polynomial is
\[
p_{A}(\lambda)=\det\!\begin{pmatrix}a-\lambda&b\\c&d-\lambda\end{pmatrix}
=(a-\lambda)(d-\lambda)-bc
=\lambda^{2}-(a+d)\lambda+(ad-bc).
\]
The coefficient of $\lambda$ is the negative of the trace $\operatorname{tr}(A)=a+d$, and the constant term is the determinant $\det(A)=ad-bc$.

\begin{example}
Find the characteristic polynomial of
\[
B=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
We compute
\[
\det(B-\lambda I)=\det\!\begin{pmatrix}4-\lambda&2\\1&3-\lambda\end{pmatrix}
=(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2\cdot1
=\lambda^{2}-7\lambda+10.
\]
Thus $p_{B}(\lambda)=\lambda^{2}-7\lambda+10$.
\end{example}

\subsection{Eigenvalues and eigenvectors}

An \term{eigenvalue} $\lambda$ of $A$ satisfies $p_{A}(\lambda)=0$. For each eigenvalue, an associated \term{eigenvector} $v\neq0$ solves
\[
(A-\lambda I)v=0.
\]
The set of all eigenvectors for a given $\lambda$, together with the zero vector, forms the \term{eigenspace} $E_{\lambda}=\ker(A-\lambda I)$. To find eigenvectors we substitute the eigenvalue into $A-\lambda I$ and solve the resulting homogeneous linear system.

\begin{example}
Using the matrix $B$ from the previous example, solve $p_{B}(\lambda)=0$:
\[
\lambda^{2}-7\lambda+10=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(\lambda-5)(\lambda-2)=0,
\]
so the eigenvalues are $\lambda_{1}=5$ and $\lambda_{2}=2$.

For $\lambda_{1}=5$:
\[
B-5I=\begin{pmatrix}4-5&2\\1&3-5\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Row reducing gives $-x+2y=0$, so $x=2y$. An eigenvector is $v_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

For $\lambda_{2}=2$:
\[
B-2I=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\1&1\end{pmatrix}
\]
which reduces to $x+y=0$, so $x=-y$. An eigenvector is $v_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
\end{example}

\subsection{Diagonalisation}

A matrix $A$ is \term{diagonalizable} if there exists an invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that
\[
A=PDP^{-1}.
\]
The columns of $P$ are eigenvectors of $A$, and the diagonal entries of $D$ are the corresponding eigenvalues, arranged in the same order. Diagonalisation is possible precisely when $A$ has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors; equivalently, the sum of the dimensions of its eigenspaces equals $n$.

If $A$ has $n$ distinct eigenvalues, the eigenvectors are automatically independent, and $A$ is diagonalizable. When eigenvalues repeat, we compare the \term{geometric multiplicity} (dimension of the eigenspace) with the \term{algebraic multiplicity} (multiplicity as a root of $p_{A}$). Diagonalisation fails if any eigenvalue's geometric multiplicity is smaller than its algebraic multiplicity.

\begin{example}
Consider
\[
C=\begin{pmatrix}6&2\\0&6\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The characteristic polynomial is $(6-\lambda)^{2}$, so the only eigenvalue is $\lambda=6$ with algebraic multiplicity $2$.
\[
C-6I=\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
\]
has rank $1$, giving a one dimensional eigenspace spanned by $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$. Because the geometric multiplicity $1$ is less than the algebraic multiplicity $2$, $C$ is not diagonalizable.

Now take
\[
D=\begin{pmatrix}5&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its eigenvalues are $5$ and $3$, each with multiplicity $1$. Eigenvectors are $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}$, which are independent. Hence $D$ is already diagonal and trivially diagonalizable with $P=I$.
\end{example}

\subsection{Similarity and the diagonalisation process}

Two square matrices $A$ and $B$ are \term{similar} if there exists an invertible matrix $P$ such that $B=P^{-1}AP$. Similar matrices represent the same linear transformation under different bases. Diagonalisation is a special case of similarity where the similar matrix $D$ is diagonal. The process of diagonalising $A$ therefore consists of three steps:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Compute the characteristic polynomial and find all eigenvalues.
  \item For each eigenvalue, determine a basis of its eigenspace; collect these basis vectors as columns of $P$.
  \item Form the diagonal matrix $D$ whose diagonal entries are the eigenvalues placed in the same order as their eigenvectors in $P$.
\end{enumerate}

If the collected eigenvectors form a basis of the whole space, $P$ is invertible and the similarity relation $A=PDP^{-1}$ holds. If not, the process stops and $A$ cannot be diagonalized. This viewpoint clarifies why the number of independent eigenvectors is the decisive criterion.

\begin{keytest}
\textbf{Key test.} Given a $3\times3$ matrix $M$, compute its characteristic polynomial, list all eigenvalues, and determine whether $M$ is diagonalizable by checking the number of independent eigenvectors.
\end{keytest}

\subsection{Exercises}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Find the characteristic polynomial of $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ and list its eigenvalues.
  \item For the matrix $A$ in part (a), compute a basis for each eigenspace and decide if $A$ is diagonalizable.
  \item Let $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors over the real numbers. Explain why $B$ cannot be diagonalized over $\mathbb{R}$.
  \item Show that a $2\times2$ matrix with distinct eigenvalues is always diagonalizable by constructing $P$ and $D$ explicitly.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Key terms}

\begin{tabular}{@{}p{3.6cm}p{10.4cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Term} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\midrule
Characteristic polynomial & $\det(A-\lambda I)$, a degree $n$ polynomial whose roots are the eigenvalues of $A$. \\
Eigenvalue & A scalar $\lambda$ such that $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. \\
Eigenvector & A non zero vector $v$ satisfying $(A-\lambda I)v=0$ for a given eigenvalue $\lambda$. \\
Eigenspace & The set $\ker(A-\lambda I)$, a subspace consisting of all eigenvectors for $\lambda$ together with the zero vector. \\
Diagonalizable & A matrix $A$ for which there exists an invertible $P$ with $A=PDP^{-1}$ and $D$ diagonal. \\
Algebraic multiplicity & The multiplicity of $\lambda$ as a root of the characteristic polynomial. \\
Geometric multiplicity & The dimension of the eigenspace associated with $\lambda$. \\
Similarity & A relation $B=P^{-1}AP$ indicating that $A$ and $B$ represent the same linear map in different bases. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
